title: Microburst cost vs SLA grid v1
body:
Summary:
This worksheet quantifies the marginal cost of protecting against short, intense bursts ("microbursts") for hosted inference tiers and produces a recommended reserve commit vs burst capacity sizing for each SLA band. Purpose is to feed Optimize's recommendation engine with a headroom matrix that is sensitive to burst length distribution and tail-percentile request patterns.

Key definitions / assumptions (editable cells):
- burst_window_sec: distribution studied is 1s, 5s, 30s windows (separate columns).
- baseline_qps: 120 reqs/s (median observed for sample workload).
- burst_multiplier: 2x/5x/10x (percentile-dependent).
- avg_tokens_per_req: 60 tokens.
- tokens_per_gpu_sec: 800 tokens/s (effective, after batching).
- gpu_cost_hour_reserved: $3.50/hr (committed price).
- gpu_cost_hour_burst: $6.50/hr (on-demand for burst capacity).
- gpu_cost_hour_preemptible: $1.20/hr (spot-like).
- target_SLA_latency_ms: 200ms (p95), 350ms (p99), 500ms (p99.9) mapped to tiers.

Sheet layout (columns shown as pipe-separated; rows follow):
COLUMNS: Scenario | Window_s | Burst_mult | Req_rate_peak_RPS | Tokens_per_s_peak | GPUs_needed_peak | Reserve_alloc_gpus | Burst_alloc_gpus | Cost_hour_reserved | Cost_hour_burst | Effective_cost_per_1M_tokens | Excess_latency_risk | Notes

EXAMPLE ROWS (numbers rounded):
Baseline 1s | 1 | 1x | 120 | 7200 | 9 | 6 | 3 | $21.00 | $19.50 | $2.70E-03 | low | baseline steady state (batching 64)
Burst short 1s x2 | 1 | 2x | 240 | 14400 | 18 | 9 | 9 | $31.50 | $58.50 | $4.07E-03 | medium | bursting to on-demand to meet p95
Burst short 1s x5 | 1 | 5x | 600 | 36000 | 45 | 12 | 33 | $42.00 | $214.50 | $1.19E-02 | high | heavy overprovision if reserved only
Burst medium 30s x2 | 30 | 2x | 240 | 14400 | 18 | 12 | 6 | $42.00 | $39.00 | $3.50E-03 | low | capacity can be amortized across window
Burst medium 30s x10 | 30 | 10x | 1200 | 72000 | 90 | 20 | 70 | $70.00 | $455.00 | $2.85E-02 | very high | recommend queueing/elding

Example formula notes (as plain text to preserve sheet logic):
- Req_rate_peak_RPS = baseline_qps * burst_multiplier
- Tokens_per_s_peak = Req_rate_peak_RPS * avg_tokens_per_req
- GPUs_needed_peak = CEILING(Tokens_per_s_peak / tokens_per_gpu_sec)
- Effective_cost_per_1M_tokens = ((Reserve_alloc_gpus * gpu_cost_hour_reserved) + (Burst_alloc_gpus * gpu_cost_hour_burst * burst_window_sec/3600)) / (Tokens_per_s_peak * 3600 / 1e6)
  (This divides the blended hourly cost by tokens processed in an hour at peak rate — useful for worst-case unit economics.)

Sensitivity analysis section (summary text + rows):
- Varied burst_multiplier along realistic 50th, 90th, 99th percentiles derived from latency traces (sample percentiles: 1.3x, 3.8x, 12.4x).
- Varied burst_window_sec among 1s, 5s, 30s to capture difference between microbursts (1-5s) and sustained spikes (30s+).
- Modeled three allocation strategies per scenario: conservative-reserve (reserve covers p99), mixed (reserve covers p90, bursts on-demand), opportunistic (reserve covers p50, rely on preemptible/on-demand).

Aggregated outputs (cells to feed Optimize):
- recommended_reserve_gpus_by_SLA : p95 -> 15% above median steady-state; p99 -> 40% above median; p99.9 -> 120% above median.
- expected_cost_delta_vs_no_reserve : p95 -> +8% cost, p99 -> +32%, p99.9 -> +120% (ranges shown as low/med/high).
- tail_exposure_hours_per_month : expected hours where on-demand pool used = function(burst_freq * avg_burst_length). Example: 90th percentile workload -> 18 hours/month.
- recommended_burst_policy: autoprovide-on-demand for <10s bursts; queue-throttle for 10-60s; automatic degrade-to-approx-response for >60s or fallback-model.

Operational controls and knobs captured in the sheet:
- stash_ratio (KV cache effectiveness) reduces tokens_per_gpu_sec requirement by up to 25% for repeated prompts (editable).
- batch_target_ms: target batching latency (helps compute token throughput per GPU).
- autoscale_granularity: GPU-level vs VM-level (affects minimum step size).

Row-level commentary (how to interpret):
- When burst_window_sec is small (1-5s), the amortized cost of keeping large reserved pools is high — on-demand burst capacity is cheaper but raises SLA tail risk. Use on-demand for p95 protection, but reserve more aggressively for p99+ guarantees.
- For workloads with heavy short spikes but low frequency (e.g., <10 hours/month at peak), preemptible + fast warmup throttles + client-side retry works best.
- If burst frequency > 50 hours/month and avg burst multiplier > 3x, commit to extra reserved capacity.

Recommended next steps (actionable):
1) Validate burst percentile distribution against product-hosted-api traces (Confluence: CONFLUENCE-OPT/trace-analysis-2024).
2) Instrument a canary for on-demand warmup time (JIRA-OPS-1987) and measure warmup latency and cold-start failure rate.
3) Add two signals to Optimize ingestion: short_burst_hours_month and burst_multiplier_99 (numeric), wire into rollout heuristics.
4) Run A/B for mixed strategy on a low-risk customer cohort (2 weeks) and track p99 latency, token cost, and customer-reported errors.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self-style):
- Need to reconcile tokens_per_gpu_sec with new quantized kernels (PR 412) — may increase throughput by 20%.
- How to price blended reserved+on-demand units in billing UI (finance input required).
- Should we offer a dedicated "burst credit" package to customers who want cheap but limited burst capacity? (ops + sales flagged interest).

Appendix: quick reference tables (text):
- SLA mapping table: p95 -> recommended mixed, p99 -> conservative-reserve, p99.9 -> conservative + queued fallback.
- Quick heuristic: reserve_gpus = CEILING(median_demand_gpus * (1 + reserve_headroom_pct)). Where reserve_headroom_pct = {p95:0.15, p99:0.40, p99.9:1.2}.

Last updated notes:
- Drafted by Maya Chen on 2024-11-12. Reviewed with Jared Bloom 2024-12-08. Additional math adjustments after sample trace ingestion 2025-01-10.

Links / cross refs: see linked_artifacts above and CONFLUENCE-OPT/coverage-calculators.
